It's lunch break; blue sky and birdsong spill through the classroom windows.
Hey, were you even listening in science class today?
That earthquake talk was kind of scary, right?
Yeah, but when the teacher called it the "Earth's breath," it sounded kind of romantic, didn't it?
Romantic? Seriously? (laughs) You're such a weirdo.
Still, imagining Earth as a living thing is kind of interesting.
If it's really breathing, we're just tiny creatures living on top of it.
Breathe or not, we're already specks to begin with.
...Huh? Did it just shake?
Yeah, but it'll stop if we wait a bit, right?
Wait... why isn't it stopping...?
Whoa! The bookshelf fell!
No way!? I've never felt it this strong—!
Get under the desks! Hurry!
[The shaking subsides.]
The tremor grows wilder—blackboards crash down, ceiling lights shatter, and screams fill the room.
Kyaa! The ceiling! Somebody help!
This door won't open! Somebody!
A violent crash erupts; windows shatter and the walls begin to crumble.
In that instant, a slab from the ceiling grazes Minato's shoulder; she cries out and collapses unconscious.
Minato!? Hang on! Minato!
His hands shaking, the protagonist grips hers. Amid the roar, only his heartbeat rings clear.
(I have to save her. Someone, please...!)
Then, a blinding light erupts from his hand, swallowing the collapsing classroom.
Sight warps and sound fades. When {name} opens their eyes again, they're inside a stark white facility.
Where... are we? Minato...! Are you okay?
...Y-yeah... This isn't school, is it...?
He looks up to see a man standing before them.
And this place is...?
Welcome to G-Lab.
Inside the white room, countless monitors glow blue while machinery hums in the stillness.
Calm down. This is G-Lab—a facility dedicated to geology and crustal shifts.
You call it a lab... so can we go home now?
You can, but first I need you to see a video.
Kaede presses a remote and news footage flares onto the wall.
"Breaking news: a quake in downtown Sendai has toppled numerous buildings, and aftershocks continue—"
No way... that's our city, isn't it...?
...Is my house okay...? Mom...!
He fumbles for his phone, which starts to vibrate.
Huh...!? It's Mom...!
[Incoming call]
Hello!? Are you okay!? I saw the news and nearly panicked to death...!
Yeah! I'm safe! I'm taking shelter... Are you alright!?
The house took some damage, but we're alright. I'm so relieved...!
Relief softens her voice after a brief silence.
Come home soon, okay? Where are you?
Just as he opens his mouth, Kaede steps in and gently takes the phone.
H-hey, Kaede!?
—Hello, pardon the intrusion. I'm Kaede, a researcher at G-Lab.
Uh? I-I see...?
During the quake your child exhibited an unusual response. We'd like to request short-term cooperation to investigate.
What? You want a middle-schooler involved in research...?
It will be in a controlled environment. This could help prevent future quakes. If his "sense" ties to crustal changes, it might save lives.
Kaede's tone stays calm, yet earnest heat seeps through.
...If it's that important... but it won't be dangerous, right?
Rest assured, we'll take full responsibility for his safety and accommodations.
After a pause, his mother's sigh comes through.
...Alright. But please let him rest properly.
Thank you. We'll take good care of him.
Kaede hands the phone back.
.........Uh. Wait, what just happened?
Your mom's surprisingly quick on the uptake. (laughs)
I didn't know my parents would agree that fast!?
Heh, that helps. We'll be counting on you.
Now then, let me explain what comes next.
Kaede hands them a pair of devices.
This is a rock hammer for collecting samples.
And this is the Phase Shifter—it stabilizes your ability.
Phase Shifter...?
In short, it keeps your spatial hops under control so you can travel safely between G-Lab and outside.
So we're really going to be doing geo research now...
Of course; it's a job that saves lives... What's wrong, not up for it?
Huh? Not happening!
Wow, Kaede knows exactly how to rile you up.
Heh, as long as you're motivated.
Then let's kick off your first mission: use the rock hammer to collect thin-section samples.
Ready? Then try using the Phase Shifter.
Is this really going to help...? I'm more worried about staying alive.
Knew you'd chicken out.
Relax. I promised you and your mom we'd keep you safe.
Alright, alright... guess I'm doing this.
Activate the Phase Shifter.
When {name} opens their eyes again, they're already outdoors.
You arrived safely. Let's start the collection mission.
See the markers on the ground? Follow them and grab the samples.
Wind scours the desolate ground.
{name} stands at the outcrop near the mountain base, gear case on their back as the terminal light flickers to connect with the lab.
Lab here. Audio and video okay? Sounds windy over there.
Loud and clear. Still a bit dusty, and the sky's gray... definitely feels post-quake.
Feed's up. Whoa, you're covered in mud. Did you bring rubber boots?
...I did, but I'm already ankle-deep. Ugh, washing these will be a pain.
Focus. That's the closest outcrop to the hypocenter, so get us a sample.
{name} pulls out the rock hammer, tapping carefully as the dry clinks vanish into the wind.
He crouches, prying fragments from the fissure into small cases while a crow caws somewhere in the distance.
Ooh, look at those bands. That powdery part totally looks like crushed cookies.
Earth desserts, huh... but it feels kinda soft for rock.
Interesting. Might be what shattered during the quake. Bring it back for thin sections.
As the case clicks shut, the ground lets out a low groan. The wind dies, and the air turns heavy.
...Did it just shake?
No... probably just nerves—
[Ground rumbling]
He doesn't finish before the ground erupts, the roar splitting his ears as the rock crumbles beneath him.
Lab to field! {name}, evacuate now! The fault's moving!
Whoa...! The Phase Shifter... where is it...!
Staggering through the shaking, he claws for the device at his waist as alarms blare and the sky splits with thunder.
{name}! Hurry! The cliff—!
[Distant collapse]
Come on, please... work!
[Teleport flash]
White light engulfs him. A heartbeat later, the deafening rumble is gone, leaving only silence and the hum of machinery.
When he comes to, he's back in the G-Lab transfer room, panting as he sets the sample on the table.
Hah... hah... I'm back... This is... the thin section I grabbed.
{name}! Are you okay!?
...I'm not scared at all!!
Who could've imagined two huge quakes in a single day!
It was rough... but I'm glad it was you out there, {name}.
If we sent someone who couldn't use the Phase Shifter, I don't even want to imagine the outcome.
You wrapped up a dangerous mission. Nice work.
Now let's analyze the sample.
The feed shifts to the lit lab. Through the monitor, the microscopic world comes into view.
Wow, everything's crushed so fine... Is that stress marks?
Right. The question is when that stress happened.
Wasn't it during the quake?
Maybe. Yet the deformation looks a bit "too fresh."
What do you mean by too fresh?
We assume the quake ended, but what if something underground is still shifting...?
...Then next we investigate below ground, right?
Exactly. Let's prep a boring survey. The deeper we drill, the more current movement we can read.
The call drops, leaving only mountain winds. He exhales and looks over the distant city, sensing Earth is still quietly shifting beneath the calm.
Boring rig prepped! You're up next, {name}!
...We have to head out again? Just thinking about that cliff makes my legs shake.
Being scared is good; it means you'll be careful. We've added triple safety this time.
And the Phase Shifter's been upgraded—99.8% transfer accuracy!
That remaining 0.2% sounds scary... but fine, I trust you.
We'll drill directly beneath the offset layer from last time, about 50 meters down.
The transfer device fires up, white light wrapping him as the scenery shifts in a blink.
Unlike the previous outcrop, the ground is eerily still—no birds, not even a breeze.
He's standing just north of where the cliff collapsed; the cracked earth is dry with faint scorch marks.
...The air feels different. It's like the world is mute.
Feed's in. Yikes, it's so quiet it's creepy.
This spot sits right above that shifted layer, close to the heart of the tremor.
Copy. I'll grab the samples and head back.
He opens the kit, secures the device, and a sliver of light through the gray clouds highlights the fissures.
...Hey, that line looks longer now.
Might not be your imagination. The soil looks wetter too.
Maybe subsurface water is moving. Either way, safety first.
He carefully scoops the topsoil into the sample container when a low sound echoes, as if something underground sighed.
...Did you hear that?
Yeah, the mic picked it up too. Definitely not wind.
Stay alert. Once it's secured, return immediately.
{name} nods, packs up the gear, and activates the Phase Shifter back to G-Lab.
The rig's vibration stops; the core pulled from underground glints coldly.
Sample acquired! Sent the log from the recommended unit too.
Nice work. Seal it on-site and keep it at temperature; log the pressure too.
Roger. Prepping to return.
Only the cooling fans whisper while the sky blushing faintly overhead.
Welcome back! You didn't fall off a cliff, right?
Haha, barely. My boots are mud again though.
Glad you're safe. Phase Shifter logs look clean too.
Here's the sample. Felt kind of odd, though...
I see. Let's take a look.
The sample rests on the analyzer as scanner light sweeps by.
...Look, Sensei, down here. Only the lower grains got crushed.
You're right... and the grains align. Classic lateral shearing.
So something beneath the surface slipped?
Exactly—and we didn't see this right after the quake.
Then does that mean it's still moving?
The data on the monitor trembles, the graph warps, and red zones widen.
...That's the fault "breathing." The ground under Sendai might not be asleep.
...The fault is alive...?
A "breathing fault" looks calm on the surface but still loads and releases stress underneath—it's active.
It might lie dormant for decades but it's still alive, so we can't let our guard down.
...The earth feeling alive is both terrifying and a little heartbreaking.
The room goes still as the sunset sinks between the buildings outside.
Still, we need clearer data to prove what's happening beneath these strata.
Surface observations alone won't cut it anymore. The "breathing" may be deeper down.
So next we literally look underground?
Right. Places people can't reach need mechanical eyes—unmanned probe drones.
Using drones to chase faults sounds exciting... but is it safe?
Can't say zero risk, but it's safer than field sampling—you won't have to go outside.
But this mission is just as important; it could save lives too.
All three gaze at the red line on the map, stretching beneath Sendai as if guarding untold truths.
Night settles over G-Lab as rain starts outside; distant lightning flashes while monitor glow bathes the lab.
The new drone unit is ready. It's not a normal drone—it's the Phase Radar Swarm prototype.
Phase radar swarm?
Right. A dozen mini drones slip into cracks and waterways, mapping underground structures with EM waves.
So basically we can scan the inside of the earth! Like a planetary CT.
...That's amazing. So we'll actually see the fault's shape?
In theory. But if the signal's too strong, groundwater reflects it and adds noise, so be careful.
{name}, we're counting on you to pilot them.
Got it... Wait, I have to control all dozen by myself?
Of course. Let's give it a shot!
(Inner voice) Kaede-sensei is so pushy...
...Did the ground just shake?
Drone activation sequence start. A dozen mini drones blink blue as they rise.
Wow... gorgeous. Like a flock of fireflies.
Totally. Can't believe we're flying all of them... I'm nervous now.
Hehe, commander debut. Don't crash them, okay?
Jokes aside. Drone swarm, begin linking to the subsurface radar system.
Communication lines streak across the monitors as each drone slips into cracks, their blue lights disappearing underground.
Checking signals from drones 1 through 8 first.
Depth 10 meters... 15... Uh-oh, drone 9's throwing noise!
Feed's up! ...What is that? A red line running under the ground?
...That's the fault plane. But it's way shallower than expected.
If it's that shallow... doesn't that put it near the city's infrastructure?
The display switches to a Sendai map, fault lines crawling beneath the city.
...It stretches all the way under Sendai Station.
And it branches! Two lines? No, three?
...Branch faults. I didn't expect them to spread this far...
The waveform suddenly spikes and red alerts flash.
What is that!? The waveform's moving—in real time!
No way... is it still slipping!?
Hold on... Sensei, it looks like a seismogram, and the period's short.
A short period means stress is building. This isn't a warning—it's the next quake beginning.
On the map, the red lines spread across Sendai with G-Lab blinking at the center.
No way... we're right on top of the fault!?
...Not just G-Lab. All of central Sendai is sitting on this awakening fault.
Then... the next thing coming is the main shock...
Thunder cracks and rain lashes harder outside as the lab lights flicker.
...Everyone, listen. We can't hide this anymore. We have to tell the government and the public.
Exactly. This research can save lives!
...Understood. Our next mission is to warn them.
The three nod in silence. On the monitor, the pulsing red fault line glows as if the earth itself is breathing.

A classroom at lunch break. Suddenly, a violent shaking strikes.
Whoa...!? An earthquake...! Everyone, get under your desks!
The shaking grows stronger, the ceiling collapses. A white light swallows your vision——.
When you wake, you are in a white laboratory you have never seen before.
Awake? This is G-Lab — a disaster-prevention institute that studies the earth to protect this town. I'm Kaede, a researcher here.
That earthquake stirred a 'power' inside you. Don't overthink it — it's the power to read the strata. Just someone who can truly listen to the voice of the land. That's all.
Thank you. To read this 'book' called the strata, first you need to know how it was written.
From mountain rock to a stratum — what's the correct order?
Weathering → Erosion → Transport → Deposition
Deposition → Transport → Erosion → Weathering
Erosion → Weathering → Deposition → Transport
Correct! Rock crumbles, is scraped away, carried, then piles up. That order is the basics.
Looking good! Then out to the field — let's turn the land's very first page with your own hands.
A field outcrop. Striped strata are visible in the ground cracked open by the quake.
Take a sample with the hammer, then check the grain size under the microscope.
So — this sample's grains are smaller than 0.06mm, smooth to the touch. What is it?
Mudstone
Sandstone
Conglomerate
Correct! The finer the grains, the farther from the river mouth and the deeper the sea where they settled. Which means this place was once a quiet, deep seabed.
The next sample — dilute hydrochloric acid produced bubbles (CO₂). What is it?
Limestone
Chert
Tuff
Right. Limestone forms from shells and coral, and releases carbon dioxide with acid. In other words, this was once a warm, shallow sea.
One more. So hard a nail can't even scratch it. What is it?
Chert
Mudstone
Conglomerate
Correct! Chert forms from the shells of tiny sea creatures and is very hard — built up by an ancient ocean over millions of years.
You noticed? That's the very thing that's been bothering me. Let's dig deeper and make sure.
We have the drill tower sample. Let's read the depth-by-depth record as a columnar section.
A fossil was found inside the rock from one of the deeper samples.
...So, what environment do you think this layer formed in?
A warm, shallow sea
A cold, deep sea
Where river and sea water mix
Correct! The fossil told us the environment of the time.
A fossil like coral that tells us the environment a layer formed in — what's it called?
Facies fossil
Index fossil
Right. A facies fossil indicates environment. A clam (Shijimi) means where river and sea mix.
...So, which era did this layer form in?
Mesozoic
Paleozoic
Cenozoic
Correct! The ammonite is a Mesozoic index fossil. The trilobite would be Paleozoic.
A fossil like the ammonite — what's it called?
Index fossil
Facies fossil
Yes. Organisms that lived widely but thrived only briefly make good index fossils.
The column has a layer of tuff, formed from compacted volcanic ash. What happened back then?
A volcano erupted nearby
A large earthquake occurred
The sea dried up
Correct! A tuff layer is evidence of a volcanic eruption in that era.
Lastly, let's compare the columns from sites A, B and C.
So — the ash layer is deeper the farther east we go. Which way do the strata tilt?
East
West
